Gueydan — William [Guillermo] Gueydan de Roussel (1908–1996), Swiss jurist and Germanist, and a friend of Schmitt since 1933.
To escape prosecution for his wartime collaboration in Paris, Gueydan moved to Argentina in 1948.
Count Yorck’s remark to Dilthey — See Briefwechsel zwischen Wilhelm Dilthey und dem Grafen Paul Yorck von Wartenburg 1877–1897, Halle an der Saale 1923, reprinted 1995.
The remark occurs in Count Yorck’s 122nd letter to Dilthey, dated 21 October 1895.
Heidegger quotes it in Being and Time, 8th unchanged ed., Tübingen 1957, p. 400.
Canonization of Robert Bellarmine — See the entry for 17 September 1947.
Essays by Pérez Bueno — P. Bueno (1877–1934), jurist. The quotation appears in Madrid científico, July 1923, p. 216.
O mors, ero mors tua; morsus tuus ero, inferne — Vulgate, Hosea 13:14. Luther: “Death, I will be poison to you; realm of the dead, I will be a plague to you.”
innocens Deus occisus — “The innocent God was killed.”

Vialatoux — Joseph Vialatoux (1880–1970), French philosopher and scholar of Hobbes. Schmitt is referring to J. Vialatoux, La Cité de Hobbes. Théorie de l’état totalitaire. Essai sur la conception naturaliste de la civilisation, Paris 1935. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 23082.

De nobis ipsis silemus, jurisconsulti — “We jurists shall keep silent about ourselves.” An adaptation of the motto by Alberico Gentili quoted on p. 79. See also the motto on the cover of Book II of the Glossarium.
by Max Weber, using a few crudely inadequate concepts — See Max Weber, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft, study edition, ed. Johannes Winckelmann, Cologne/Berlin 1964, first half-volume, pp. 397 ff.

The end of Masaryk’s son — Jan Masaryk (1886–1948), Czechoslovak foreign minister, was found dead beneath the window of his official residence. His death was officially declared a suicide; according to later findings, he was murdered by the Communist secret service. His father, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk (1850–1937), was a co-founder and the first president of Czechoslovakia.

like Joseph de Maistre’s parents in 1772 — This does not refer to 1772, but to 1763. The final suppression of the Jesuit order in 1773 was preceded by a series of repressive measures. One of these was the French Parlement’s decision in 1763 to close the Jesuit schools and force the Jesuit fathers to renounce their religious vows.
An anecdote connected with this episode says that de Maistre’s mother once spoke sternly to her exuberantly playful nine-year-old son:
“Joseph, don’t be so cheerful; something terrible has happened!”
De Maistre is said to have remembered those words for the rest of his life.
See Robert Triomphe, Joseph de Maistre. Études sur la vie et sur la doctrine d’un matérialiste mystique, Geneva 1968, p. 71.

The Grewe-Küster discussion — Wilhelm Grewe/Otto Küster, Nürnberg als Rechtsfrage. Eine Diskussion / Stuttgart Private Study Society. Main speaker: Wilhelm Grewe. Respondent: Otto Küster. Stuttgart 1947.
Wilhelm Grewe (1911–2000), scholar of international law and diplomat, was a student of Forsthoff and had known Schmitt since 1931. Seven letters and one telegram survive in Schmitt’s papers.
my legal opinion from the summer of 1945 — Angriffskrieg (War of Aggression).
Tu quoque — “You too.” A way of rejecting an accusation by pointing out that the accuser has behaved in the same way. The argument played a certain part in the Nuremberg war-crimes trials.

Max Weber’s diagnosis and prognosis — See Max Weber, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft, study edition, ed. Johannes Winckelmann, Cologne/Berlin 1964, first half-volume, p. 656. Schmitt omits part of the first sentence. In Winckelmann’s edition, the wording of the quotation that follows is also different.
Friedrich Engels in the posthumously published work — F. Engels, Die Rolle der Gewalt in der Geschichte, in Karl Marx/Friedrich Engels, Werke, Vol. 21, Berlin 1979, p. 434.
That is my beloved Bruno Bauer quotation — See the note below to p. 236.
Veronica — Veronica Runte-Schranz (1924–2007), daughter of Dr. Franz Schranz of Siedlinghausen, a physician and friend of Carl Schmitt.
veritas in verbo (dicto) non in re — Correctly: veritas enim in dicto, non in re consistit: “Truth lies in what is said, not in things.”
Thomas Hobbes, De corpore, ch. III.7, in Opera latina I, London 1839, p. 31.

Rudenko’s shot at Göring — During the Nuremberg war-crimes trials, the chief Soviet prosecutor, Roman Andreyevich Rudenko (1907–1981), wanted the murder of the Polish officers at Katyn to be punished as a German crime.
During the hearing on the matter, Göring accused the Soviet Union of being responsible. Rudenko is then said to have flown into a rage and fired two pistol shots at Göring.
Historians have not confirmed the story.
See Joe J. Heydecker/Johannes Leeb, Der Nürnberger Prozeß, Cologne 2003, p. 450.
the great Cisneros — Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros (1436–1517), Spanish cardinal and patron of humanist learning.

Nam a civilibus et forensibus studiis … — “For his nature had been so repelled by studies of constitutional and courtroom law that, as many reliable people said they had heard, whatever he took in from that discipline he immediately vomited back up.”
The passage appears word for word in Nomos, p. 79, footnote. The work mentioned below is also cited there.
Marcel Bataillon — M. Bataillon, Érasme et l’Espagne. Recherches sur l’histoire spirituelle du 16e siècle, Paris 1937; reprinted Geneva 1998, here p. 14.
I am now more than Thomas Masaryk — See above, p. 85.
Found a note from 14 December 1913 — See Tb 1912–15, p. 127, note 46.
Gregor. Thaumat. — Gregory Thaumaturgus, or Gregorios Thaumaturgos (c. 210–270), Greek theologian and bishop from Asia Minor.
not δογματικῶς, but ἀγνωστικῶς — “not with knowledge of the doctrine, but in ignorance.”
Hermann Kasack, Wilhelm Ahlmann — The blind banker and jurist Wilhelm Ahlmann (1895–1944) belonged to the resistance against Hitler. On 7 September 1944 he committed suicide to avoid arrest.
Schmitt, who had been his friend, dedicated Ex Captivitate Salus to him in 1950 and also contributed to the 1951 memorial volume for Ahlmann.
In Hermann Kasack’s novel Die Stadt hinter dem Strom (1947), Ahlmann appears as the “Lübeck merchant Dr. Hahn.” Kasack also contributed an essay under that title to the memorial volume.

See Tymbos für Wilhelm Ahlmann, Berlin 1951, pp. 127–134 for Kasack and pp. 244–251 for Schmitt. Schmitt’s copy, containing annotations, inserted material, and pasted-in newspaper clippings, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 28355.
Pascual Jordan — (1902–1980), theoretical physicist. Three letters survive in Schmitt’s papers.
δός μοι ποῦ στῶ — Δός μοι ποῦ στῶ καὶ τὴν γῆν κινήσω: “Give me a fixed point outside the earth, and I will move the earth.”
A saying attributed to Archimedes, used to illustrate his law of the lever.
Stare decisis — “Stand by earlier decisions.” A principle of Anglo-American case law.
my lecture of February 1941 — “Staatliche Souveränität und freies Meer.” Most recently published with an extensive commentary by G. Maschke in SGN, pp. 401–430.
Introduction to Thucydides — Schmitt owned the following edition: Thucydides, Der große Krieg, translated and introduced by Heinrich Weinstock, Kröner pocket edition 150, Stuttgart 1938.
“annihilated in nothing” — “Defenseless, but in no way destroyed.”
From the opening poem titled “1933” in Konrad Weiß, Der christliche Epimetheus, Berlin 1933.
Dominus litis — “Master of the proceedings,” a legal term.

A Nation can only be condemned out of her own mouth — A reference to the English documentation of German war crimes during the First World War: H. W. Wilson, Convicted out of her own mouth. The record of German crimes, London 1917. German edition: Durch das Zeugnis des eigenen Mundes überführt, no place or date, c. 1918.
Schmitt probably became familiar with the book, in effect as part of his professional duties, while working for the Bavarian military command.
pèlerin de l’Absolu — Le Pèlerin de l’Absolu (“The Pilgrim of the Absolute”), the title of a volume of diaries by Léon Bloy.
CIC — Civil Internment Camp, the Allied camps established from 1945 onward for suspected or potential war criminals.
“Hic jacet” is the finishing part of his [correctly: their] history — Daniel Defoe, The Instability of Human Glory.

The ashes will not rest; they scatter through every land — After Jan Hus was burned as a heretic at Constance in 1415 and his ashes were thrown into the Rhine, a song arose among his followers. It begins:
The ashes will not settle down, They scatter through every land; No stream or pit or grave can help— They bring the enemy to shame!
Schmitt quotes this song in a letter to Jünger in connection with a funeral ceremony in Rome at which ashes were thrown into the Tiber.
my περίψημα-existence — See the note above to p. 23.

Arnold Toynbee (Int. Affairs, Nov. 47) — Arnold Toynbee (1889–1975), British historian and theorist of civilization. Schmitt is referring to Toynbee’s article in The International Outlook, Vol. 23, No. 4, October 1947, pp. 463–476.
Claudel discovers … — Paul Claudel, “Quelques réflexions sur l’Allemagne,” in A présent, 19 March 1948.

Biographical introduction — To: Thomas Hobbes, The Moral and Political Works Of Thomas Hobbes Of Malmesbury. Never before collected together. To which is prefixed, The Author’s Life, Extracted From That said to be written by Himself, As Also From The Supplement to the said Life by Dr. Blackbourne [Richard Blackburne]; and farther illustrated by the Editor, with Historical and Critical Remarks on his Writings and Opinions, London 1750.
Schmitt owned this edition, RW 265 No. 24285.
Blötz — Ferdinand Blötz (1901–1967), Hamburg jurist, later a senior judge at the Regional Court there.

Eugen Ott — (1889–1977), general and diplomat. As an adviser to the Schleicher government in 1932–33 he worked closely with Schmitt. In 1933 he first became military attaché; from 1938 he served as ambassador to Japan. In 1942, in connection with the affair surrounding the spy Richard Sorge, he was recalled from his ambassadorial post and withdrew to Beijing. From 1951 onward he lived in retirement in Tutzing.
Spiegel on Sorge — A multi-part series on the spy Richard Sorge in Der Spiegel, 1951, issues 24–40.
To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 222 f.

Sohm II — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Rudolf Sohm, Kirchenrecht (= Systematisches Handbuch der deutschen Rechtswissenschaft, ed. Karl Binding, Vol. 8), anastatic reprint, Munich/Leipzig 1923.
Vol. 1: Die geschichtlichen Grundlagen. Vol. 2: Katholisches Kirchenrecht.
Copies survive in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 Nos. 25085 and 25336.

Conde — Francisco Javier Conde (1908–1974), Spanish political scientist who moved politically from socialism to Francoism. Conde studied under both Hermann Heller and Carl Schmitt and translated Schmitt’s The Concept of the Political and Leviathan.
Schmitt is probably referring to their meeting in Madrid in 1943, where Conde had been a professor since 1942.
Conde died while serving as Spanish ambassador in Bonn.
Naturales deos colere cupis, civiles cogeris — “You wish to worship the gods of nature, but you are compelled to worship the gods of the state.”
Augustine, De civitate Dei, Book 6, ch. 6. Translation based on the German edition: Augustine, Vom Gottesstaat, translated from the Latin by Wilhelm Thimme, Vol. 1, Munich 1977, p. 295.
your essay — Helmut Rumpf, “Deutschlands Anschluß. Voraussetzungen für die Einigung,” in Volk und Zeit. Monatszeitschrift für Demokratie und Sozialismus 3, 1948, pp. 58–60.
what E. Troeltsch said about it —

“The Christian theory of natural law is, as a scientific theory, wretched and confused. Within it, the pure natural law of humanity’s original state constantly collides with the completely opposite relative natural law of the fallen state; with positive law, which often includes the worst atrocities; and with a supreme theocratic authority which, despite everything, claims that true goodness can only be communicated through itself. But as a practical doctrine it is of the highest importance in cultural and social history …”
Ernst Troeltsch, Die Soziallehren der christlichen Kirchen und Gruppen, third reprint of the Tübingen 1922 edition, Aalen 1977, p. 173.
Schmitt is referring to the first edition, Tübingen 1912. His annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22087.
